components.text: Explain how direct forgiveness of sincere repentance remains consistent with God's justice and holy law.
Address the asserted role of final deed accounting in the proposed direct-forgiveness model.
Whether direct forgiveness and deed accounting preserve God's holy law after it has been violated.
Whether scriptural forgiveness may occur without a ground that maintains divine holiness and law.
Answer the denial that Adam's fall has inherited or representative consequences for later humanity.
Address the appeal to Old Testament personal responsibility for each person's own conduct.
Whether Adam's rebellion affects his progeny through spiritual death despite Con's denial of inherited original sin.
Whether fallen people retain the unaided capacity assumed by a repentance-and-accounting route.
Answer the claim that forgiveness requires a ground preserving divine justice, holiness, and respect for law.
Address the claim that substitution uniquely permits mercy without undoing justice.
Whether direct forgiveness can remain consistent with God's justice and holiness when applied by a principled rule.
Whether substitution is necessary to prevent mercy from undoing justice.
Answer the claim that fallen people are so morally unable that they cannot be righteous or secure reconciliation through conduct.
Address the specific claim that people cannot come to Christ without divine drawing and liberation.
Whether humanity is so depraved that no person can be judged righteous under merciful moral accounting.
Whether the biblical record supports the absolute incapacity claimed by Pro.
Whether good deeds may have an accounting role rather than being only post-salvation fruit.
Address the internal claim that substitution coherently preserves both divine mercy and justice.
Address the distinction between deeds as salvation's fruit and deeds as its basis.
Whether substitutionary justification is historically attributable to Jesus rather than chiefly to Paul.
Whether the Pauline human-condition framework reflects original teaching or later development.
Answer the claim that good deeds are only fruits of completed salvation rather than material human participation.
Address whether divine enablement is compatible with meaningful human obligation and action.
Whether divine enablement leaves human action merely evidential or makes it an indispensable salvation obligation.
Whether God's assistance is compatible with a person's genuine obligation to act.
Answer the inference that the command to work out salvation makes human deeds part of salvation's basis.
Explain how divine transformation and required good deeds fit a salvation already possessed.
Whether working out salvation means adding to Christ's work or expressing a salvation already possessed.
Whether good deeds function as saving contributions rather than fruits of divine transformation.
Explain how Jesus can coherently be both the one offering and the sacrifice rather than an innocent external victim.
Show how Christ's priestly sacrifice relates to and surpasses the Old Testament sacrificial system.
Address whether the atonement account is merely Pauline rather than part of broader New Testament witness.
Whether Jesus is merely an innocent victim punished by another or is himself the priestly offerer and sacrifice.
Whether the atonement mechanism has substantial non-Pauline grounding in Hebrews.
Whether Christ's sacrifice coherently fulfills rather than ignores the Old Testament priestly system.
Answer the claim that people begin in inherited spiritual death and cannot return to God through repentance.
Address whether return to God requires special divine drawing and liberation.
Address whether another's effective sacrifice is necessary to restore the sinner.
Whether reconciliation requires Christ's permanently effective sacrifice rather than direct return and forgiveness.
Whether people begin spiritually fallen rather than in a naturally saved disposition.
Whether a sinner can return through repentance and restitution without special liberation.
Whether another person's payment is necessary for forgiveness.
Answer why an innocent Jesus can coherently serve as a sacrifice for other people's sin.
Address the claim that repentance and restitution suffice without another person's payment.
Address the claim that merciful deed accounting can render people righteous without atonement.
Whether an innocent substitute can coherently offer an efficacious sacrifice for the sins of others.
Whether direct repentance makes the unique sinless God-man's sacrifice unnecessary.
Whether salvation through sacrifice remains an act of God's own mercy.
Answer the historical claim that substitutionary justification is chiefly Pauline and increasingly supported only by later Gospels.
Address the claim that earlier scripture permits forgiveness without Christological substitution.
Address the proposed sufficiency of repentance, restitution, and direct forgiveness.
Whether atonement is a late Pauline development or a consistent message extending from Genesis through Revelation.
Whether God's own provided means of reconciliation preserves holiness and justice better than direct human return.
Whether Old Testament forgiveness belongs within a continuous sacrificial reconciliation pattern.
Whether humanly proposed repentance and return can replace God's provided reconciliatory means.
